title: A Rare Presentation of Lupus Nephritis: Postpartum Complement-Mediated Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome Mimicking Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura.
abstract: Complement-mediated hemolytic uremic syndrome (CM-HUS) is a rare form of thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) that may complicate systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and can be difficult to distinguish from thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), because both present with thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, and end-organ injury. We report a 21-year-old woman with obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, hypertriglyceridemia, and a positive antinuclear antibody who presented four months postpartum with nausea, vomiting, headache, and facial swelling. Evaluation revealed severe hypertension, anemia, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury, nephrotic-range proteinuria, and hematuria, and a peripheral smear showed schistocytes consistent with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. Given concern for TTP, she underwent therapeutic plasma exchange and received high-dose corticosteroids with initial improvement. Further workup demonstrated markedly elevated anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies, profound hypocomplementemia, and biopsy-proven Class III lupus nephritis with thrombotic microangiopathy, while ADAMTS13 activity was preserved at 94%, effectively excluding TTP and supporting lupus-associated CM-HUS. Plasma exchange was discontinued and the patient was treated with hydroxychloroquine, mycophenolate mofetil, tacrolimus, and corticosteroids; complement inhibition with eculizumab was deferred given an ongoing response. At follow-up, platelet count and renal function normalized and hemoglobin stabilized on immunosuppression alone. Pregnancy and the postpartum period are recognized complement-amplifying states that may precipitate endothelial injury and unmask autoimmune disease. This case underscores that preserved ADAMTS13 activity, active lupus serologies, hypocomplementemia, and biopsy-proven lupus nephritis are critical to distinguishing CM-HUS from TTP and to guiding lupus-directed therapy that can achieve favorable hematologic and renal recovery.
journal: Journal of investigative medicine high impact case reports

title: Hydroxychloroquine-Associated Renal Phospholipidosis: A Forgotten Complication of a Common Drug.
abstract: Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) treatment in systemic lupus erythematosus can induce drug-induced phospholipidosis mimicking Fabry disease. A 32-year-old woman with lupus nephritis developed podocyte "zebra bodies" on electron microscopy. Normal lyso-Gb3 excluded Fabry disease, confirming HCQ toxicity. Discontinuation and immunosuppression yielded stable renal function and improved proteinuria.

title: Gaps in care for hydroxychloroquine retinopathy screening in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus or rheumatoid arthritis: a population-based cohort study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Guideline-concordant screenings for hydroxychloroquine retinopathy (HCQ-R) are essential for safe long-term use of HCQ. We assessed adherence to the HCQ-R screening recommendations among patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and evaluated patient- and health system-level predictors of adherence.
METHODS: We conducted a longitudinal population-based cohort study (1997-2023) using linked British Columbia administrative health data capturing all physician and hospital encounters, tests billed, pharmacy-dispensed medications, and demographics. Using previously published algorithms, we identified all adults with SLE or RA who initiated HCQ after diagnosis and remained on therapy continuously for ≥ 1 year. Guideline-concordant (valid) screening was defined as a retinal visit (ICD-9 362.xx) with spectral domain optical coherence tomography and/or visual field-testing fee(s) (22067/02043) within a ± 30-day window, from baseline (HCQ initiation) until 31-Dec-2023, HCQ cessation, or censoring. Population-level adherence was assessed based on baseline and annual rates of valid screening. Patient-level adherence was assessed as the mean cumulative count of valid screenings received by each year of follow-up, with 95% CIs. Predictors of annual valid screening, including physician-care patterns (continuous vs. noncontinuous rheumatology vs. family-physician care), health authority regions, socioeconomic status (SES) and baseline screening, were assessed via multivariable generalized estimating equations adjusted for demographics and comorbidities.
RESULTS: Of the 28,301 eligible patients for screening, 24% completed a valid baseline screening within year 1; during years 2-25, the annual rate of valid screenings ranged from 20 to 35%, and 70% remained unscreened on average. By 15 years, patients received on average 2.7 (95% CI, 2.6-2.8) valid screenings compared with at least 12 expected by this time, as recommended by the guidelines. Having a baseline screening was the strongest predictor of subsequent annual screenings (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 5.71; 95% CI: 4.89-6.67). Compared with continuous rheumatology care, family physician care had lower odds of screening (aOR, 0.59; 0.49-0.72). Most regions had lower screening rates than did Vancouver Coastal Health (9.50%-24.57%), with the lowest screening rate in Island Health (aOR, 0.39; 0.30-0.51). SES was not significantly associated with the odds of receiving annual screening.
CONCLUSIONS: Guideline-recommended HCQ-R screening adherence was consistently low within a publicly funded health-care system; on average, one-fourth of patients on long-term HCQ, completed a valid screening annually. Strategies to strengthen guideline-based practices and reduce regional disparities are needed.

title: [Systemic lupus erythematosus: new treatment targets and agents].
abstract: Management of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) has moved towards a defined treat-to-target approach. In April 2025 the first German S3 guideline was published, complementing the 2023 EULAR recommendations and the 2025 EULAR update on kidney involvement. All emphasize hydroxychloroquine as a backbone, a prednisolone target of ≤5mg/day and early use of belimumab or anifrolumab without any specific preference. Two validated targets guide therapy: DORIS remission (clinical SLEDAI 0, PGA <0,5, prednisolone ≤5mg/day) and LLDAS (SLEDAI-2K ≤4 without vital organ activity, PGA ≤1, prednisolone ≤7,5mg/day). Anifrolumab has been approved for subcutaneous self-administration in the EU since December 2025. Obinutuzumab, a type II anti-CD20 antibody, met its primary endpoint in the phase III trials REGENCY and ALLEGORY. Dapirolizumab pegol enabled glucocorticoid tapering alongside BICLA response in a phase III trial. Cellular approaches are advancing: autologous CD19 CAR T cells led to long-lasting remission in the refractory SLE patients, while off-the-shelf allogeneic constructs and T-cell engagers such as teclistamab or blinatumumab are in early clinical development.
